fixes.explanation: That's an honest question, baker, but Paul doesn't raise it here. Prayer isn't what he brings up in verse 19. The question he expects is, “Then why does God still find fault? For who can resist His will?”

Right, baker. Paul asks, “Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it…” and then gives the words the formed thing would say. It's a picture of the made talking back to the maker. He sets that picture right after the question in verse 19.

That one's actually in the text, friend. Paul says, “Shall what is formed say to Him who formed it…” The picture is of the formed talking back to the One who formed it. Verse 20 even gives the words it would say: why did You make me like this.
Good try, friend, but tested isn't there. Verse 24 says God has “called” them, “…not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?” That calling is what Paul names.

Yes, friend. Paul quotes, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’…” The same place where they heard no gets a new answer. That's the promise Paul brings from Hosea.

This one is actually in the text, baker. Paul quotes, “It will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’…” Hosea's words are right there in verse 26.

Nice guess, baker, but priests aren't mentioned here. Priests don't come up in Isaiah's line at all. Isaiah says, “Though the number of the Israelites is like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved.”
Right, friend. Isaiah says, “For the Lord will carry out His sentence on the earth thoroughly and decisively.” Thoroughly and decisively, not halfway. Paul passes along Isaiah's words in verse 28.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, “Unless the Lord of Hosts had left us descendants, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” The descendants left to them make the difference. Paul says it's just as Isaiah foretold.
Babylon and Nineveh are big names, friend, but Isaiah's line names other cities. It says, “…we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” Those are the two.
Tyre and Sidon are a good try, baker, but they're not the cities in Isaiah's line. He says, “…we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” Those are the two.

Close to the letter, baker, since Rome is where Paul is sending it (Romans 1:7). But the believers in Rome are the ones receiving his words. The people he's grieving over are named in verse 4 as the people of Israel.

Right, baker. Paul says “…from them proceeds the human descent of Christ, who is God over all, forever worthy of praise! Amen.” He doesn't just stop at the family tree. He ends it with praise, and I think that tells you how he feels about Christ.
Joseph is a famous name, friend. He was Jacob's son (Genesis 35:24). But the Scripture Paul quotes is about Abraham's offspring, and it says, “Through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.”
That's right, baker. The promise says, “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” Sarah was Abraham's wife (Genesis 11:29). The promise came first, and then came Isaac.

You've got it, baker. Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” Paul says it came “…not by works but by Him who calls…” Verse 11 adds that this was said before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad.

I get the guess, friend, but Rebecca was told, “The older will serve the younger.” Paul says that came “…not by works but by Him who calls…” The younger serving the older is the other way around from what she was told.

Yes, baker. The line says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” It's a heavy line, and I think it's worth reading slowly. Paul has just said this was settled before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad.

That's it, baker. The Scripture says, “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you…” Pharaoh was the king of Egypt in Moses' day (Exodus 6:11). Power is the purpose God names there.
That would make for a very plain shelf, baker. But Paul says the potter can make “…one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?” from the same clay. So there are two uses.

That's it, baker. Paul says God “…bore with great patience the vessels of His wrath, prepared for destruction?” Patience comes attached to the wrath here, and I think that's worth slowing down for. It's right there in verse 22.
I see the logic, baker, but warned isn't in verse 24. It says God has “called” them, “…not only from the Jews, but also from the Gentiles?” Called is the word.
Yes, baker. God says in Hosea, “I will call them ‘My People’ who are not My people…” Hosea was a prophet (Hosea 1:1–2). People once called not His own get a new name from Him.
